title: Log rules and exponential equations
objective: Apply logarithm rules with valid domains and solve exponential or logarithmic equations with complete solution checks.
why: Logarithms let you undo multiplicative relationships and recover an unknown exponent. Their identities are powerful because they turn products and powers into simpler arithmetic, but every step has conditions. This lesson develops those identities, explains which rewrites preserve a complete real domain, and solves equations with exact answers and every candidate checked. These are the algebraic tools used for decay times and logarithmic scales in the next lesson.

prerequisites.label: Fractions, rational expressions, and original exclusions

sections.heading: Preserve both values and allowed inputs
paragraphs: Two real functions are the same only when they accept the same inputs and give the same value at every accepted input. A simplification can agree wherever both formulas exist while quietly changing the domain. Record the domain of each original expression before applying an identity, canceling a factor, or multiplying by zero.

For a real logarithm, the base must satisfy $b>0$ and $b\ne1$, and its complete argument must be strictly positive. In a sum of logarithms, each argument has its own positivity condition. In an equation, every expression on both sides must exist. A product of two negative factors can be positive even though the logarithm of either separate factor is undefined.

The identity $\ln(u^2)=2\ln|u|$ holds for every real u other than zero. Replacing the right side with $2\ln u$ retains only u>0. Equality on that smaller common domain is useful when that restriction is stated, but it does not preserve the entire original real function. An absolute value makes a nonzero argument positive; it never makes zero acceptable.

sections.heading: Derive product and quotient rules
paragraphs: Let $u=\log_b A$ and $v=\log_b B$, with A>0, B>0 and the same valid base b. By definition, $A=b^u$ and $B=b^v$. Multiplication gives $AB=b^{u+v}$, so $\log_b(AB)=u+v=\log_b A+\log_b B$. Adding logarithms therefore corresponds to multiplying their arguments.

Division gives $A/B=b^{u-v}$ and therefore $\log_b(A/B)=\log_b A-\log_b B$. The numerator belongs to the first logarithm and the denominator to the subtracted logarithm. Reversing the quotient changes the sign. These arguments work for bases between zero and one as well as for bases above one.

The hypotheses A>0 and B>0 ensure that both separate logarithms exist. A positive product or quotient by itself is not enough: both A and B could be negative. When starting from a logarithm of a combined variable expression, inspect its entire original domain before splitting it. Absolute-value versions can preserve values on negative-factor branches, but the original positive-product or positive-quotient restriction must still be retained.

sections.heading: Move powers and roots with their conditions
paragraphs: For A>0, write $A=b^u$ with $u=\log_b A$. Then $A^r=b^{ur}$, so $\log_b(A^r)=r\log_b A$. The exponent belongs to the entire argument being raised to a power. It becomes a signed multiplier outside the logarithm, not an exponent on the logarithm value.

A negative exponent remains negative when moved outside: $\log_b(A^{-m})=-m\log_b A$. A positive nth root contributes a reciprocal exponent: $\log_b(\sqrt[n]{A})=(1/n)\log_b A$. These statements use positive A, ensuring that the separate real logarithm and the stated real powers exist.

Do not remove the positivity hypothesis merely because a particular integer power happens to be positive. An even power of a negative number is positive, but the logarithm of the unpowered negative number is not real. For variable expressions, determine the original domain first and use an absolute value where it is needed to preserve that domain.

sections.heading: Expand even powers over the full real domain
paragraphs: For a nonzero real u, an even power satisfies $u^{2m}=|u|^{2m}>0$. Therefore $\log_b(u^{2m})=2m\log_b|u|$ on the complete domain u different from zero. The absolute value is part of the mathematical argument, not an optional decoration.

When a quotient contains even powers, exclude the denominator zeros first and exclude any numerator zeros that would make the logarithm argument zero. Away from those points, positive constants and even powers make the quotient positive. Expand the positive factors, subtract denominator logarithms, and keep each coefficient with its own absolute-value argument.

An odd positive power behaves differently: $u^{2m+1}>0$ requires u>0, so its original logarithm already has only the positive branch. In that case $(2m+1)\log_b u$ preserves the domain. The choice of an absolute value comes from the original expression and its allowed inputs, not from a rule to insert absolute values everywhere.

sections.heading: Condense on the original common domain
paragraphs: To condense a sum or difference of same-base logarithms, begin with the common domain of all original terms. Move coefficients into powers of their complete arguments, turn addition into multiplication, and turn subtraction into division. The result is one logarithm used on that recorded original domain.

The condensed argument may be positive at extra inputs where an original logarithm was undefined. An even power can remove a sign from the combined formula, and a quotient can become positive from two negative terms. Those new inputs do not become valid for the original expression merely because the condensed formula can be evaluated there.

You can verify a condensation by expanding it back under the original positivity assumptions. Keep the signs of coefficients, denominator factors and the constant factor. When a full-domain expansion is desired instead, return to the actual domain of the original combined expression and decide which absolute values and restrictions it needs.

examples.title: Equal on a shared domain is not full equivalence
examples.prompt: Compare $L(x)=\ln((x-2)^2)$ and $R(x)=2\ln(x-2)$ as complete real functions.

steps.reason: The square is positive on either side of its zero. The original logarithm accepts both branches.
The separate logarithm without absolute values requires a positive shifted input.
A single input accepted only by L demonstrates that the complete domains differ.
Use the positive absolute value to preserve the entire original domain.

examples.conclusion: L and R agree for x>2, but they are not the same complete real function. The absolute-value expansion preserves both branches.

examples.title: An absolute value preserves both branches
examples.prompt: Expand $\ln((x+1)^4)$ on its full real domain and check x=-3.

steps.reason: An even power is strictly positive precisely when its base is nonzero.
The absolute-value argument is positive on exactly the original domain, so the power identity applies there.
The negative shifted input remains valid in both the original expression and the absolute-value expansion.

examples.conclusion: The complete domain is all real x except -1. Writing 4 ln(x+1) instead would remove every input below -1.

examples.title: A product becomes a sum of logarithms

steps.reason: Both original logarithms use one valid base and positive arguments.
The product identity combines the arguments multiplicatively.
Recognize an exact power instead of introducing rounded decimals.

examples.conclusion: The exact value is 3. Adding the arguments would produce a different expression.

examples.title: A quotient keeps its order

steps.reason: Both arguments are positive. The first argument stays in the numerator.
Divide the fractions before recognizing the resulting power.
The logarithm returns the exponent of the valid base. A negative logarithm value is allowed.

examples.conclusion: The exact value is -3. Reversing the quotient would give 3 and reverse the subtraction.

examples.title: Two negative factors cannot be split into real logs
examples.prompt: Compare $\ln((x-1)(x+2))$ with $\ln(x-1)+\ln(x+2)$ at x=-3 and over their full domains.

steps.reason: The two factors have the same sign on the outside intervals. Their zeros are excluded.
The separate logarithms accept only the positive-factor branch.
The complete original argument is positive even though both factors are negative.
The proposed split does not exist at this input. The product rule cannot be applied without its individual positivity conditions.

examples.conclusion: The combined expression has domain (-inf,-2) U (1,inf), while the separate logs have domain (1,inf). A full-domain absolute-value expansion must still retain the original outside intervals.

examples.title: A negative power is a signed multiplier
examples.prompt: Evaluate $\log_5((1/25)^{-3})$ exactly using the power identity.

steps.reason: The positive unpowered argument permits the identity, and the signed exponent becomes the multiplier.
Recognize the reciprocal as an exact negative power.
The positive result also checks directly against the original argument.

examples.conclusion: The exact logarithm is 6. Moving the exponent does not erase its minus sign.

examples.title: A root contributes a reciprocal exponent

steps.reason: The positive cube root corresponds to exponent 1/3.
The exponent 2/3 converts 8 into 4.
Keep the exact fraction and check by exponentiating in the original base.

examples.conclusion: The exact value is 2/9. A root contributes a reciprocal multiplier, not multiplication by its index.

examples.title: Expand a quotient of even powers
examples.prompt: Expand $\log_2\left(\frac{8(x-1)^4}{(x+2)^2}\right)$ over its full real domain and check x=-3.

steps.reason: The denominator excludes -2, while the zero numerator at 1 is rejected by the logarithm. Elsewhere the quotient is positive.
Separate positive factors and the positive quotient on the recorded domain.
The even powers require absolute values to retain both signs of the shifted inputs.
The original expression and expansion agree on a negative-input branch that would be lost without absolute values.

examples.conclusion: The expansion is valid on all real inputs except -2 and 1. Both the coefficients and the complete original domain are part of the answer.

examples.title: An odd power keeps a positivity requirement
examples.prompt: Expand $\ln((x-3)^3)$ on its complete real domain.

steps.reason: An odd power retains the sign of its base.
The original domain already guarantees a positive unpowered argument, so no absolute value is required.
An input below 3 is not in the original domain. An absolute-value formula defined there would need the original restriction to remain equivalent.

examples.conclusion: The expansion 3 ln(x-3) preserves the original domain x>3.

examples.title: Condense coefficients into a single rational argument

steps.reason: Every separate logarithm must exist. The positive constant 5 adds no variable restriction.
Move each coefficient into a power of its complete positive argument.
Combine the numerator factors and retain the subtracted term in the denominator.

examples.conclusion: The combined argument is 5(x-1)^3/(x+2)^2, used on the original domain x>1.

examples.title: The condensed formula can accept extra inputs
examples.prompt: Condense $2\ln(x-1)-\ln(x+2)$ and compare its original domain with the new formula.

steps.reason: The original separate logarithms require x>1.
The condensation is justified on the recorded common domain.
As a new standalone formula, the condensed logarithm also accepts inputs between -2 and 1.
This probe identifies an extra input of the standalone condensed formula.

examples.conclusion: Retain x>1 when claiming equivalence to the original expression. Condensation does not authorize the extra branch.

guided.title: Complete a logarithmic equation and its candidate audit
guided.setup: Solve $\log_2(x-1)+\log_2(x-3)=3$ over the real numbers. Construct the combined argument, find every algebraic candidate, and verify the retained solution in both original logarithms.
before: Write a strict positivity condition for each original argument and intersect the two conditions.
On that common domain, the product identity combines the logarithms. Expand the argument and convert the resulting logarithm statement to an exponential statement.
Solve the complete quadratic, then check each candidate in the original arguments before selecting the solution set.

question.prompt: Complete every part of the original-domain check and equation solution. Exact equivalent numbers and expressions are accepted; the combined polynomial must be expanded.

fields.label: Original common real domain
fields.help: Use interval notation with the correct strict endpoint.

Second original argument at the retained solution

hints: Both x-1 and x-3 must be strictly positive. The stricter lower bound controls their intersection.
The combined argument is (x-1)(x-3), and its required value is 2^3. Subtract that target to form a quadratic equal to zero.
The quadratic factors as (x-5)(x+1). The candidate -1 makes both original arguments negative; the other candidate makes them 4 and 2.
explanation: The original common domain is x>3. On that interval, the sum combines into log base 2 of (x-1)(x-3).
The expanded argument is x^2-4x+3 and must equal 8. Therefore x^2-4x-5=(x-5)(x+1)=0, giving candidates 5 and -1.

At -1, the original arguments are -2 and -4, so the original logarithms are undefined. At 5, they are 4 and 2, and log base 2 of 4 plus log base 2 of 2 is 2+1=3. The complete real solution set is {5}.
question.answerSummary: Original domain (3,inf); expanded argument x^2-4x+3; target 8; candidates -1 and 5; reject -1; complete solution {5}; original arguments 4 and 2.

guided.after: This guided audit supplies support and does not award independent objective evidence. Reconstruct the argument and domain reasoning in fresh practice before attempting a checkpoint.

interaction.prompt: Compare a proposed logarithm rewrite in three stages: predict the complete domains, predict exact values at a chosen input, and explain what the probe can and cannot establish. Keep a claim about one input separate from a claim about every permitted input.

summary: Use a positive logarithm base other than one and a strictly positive complete argument. Every separate logarithm and every original denominator contributes a condition.
For positive A and B in the same valid base, $\log_b(AB)=\log_b A+\log_b B$ and $\log_b(A/B)=\log_b A-\log_b B$. A power of a positive argument gives $\log_b(A^r)=r\log_b A$.
Preserve the full real domain when expanding even powers: $\ln(u^2)=2\ln|u|$ for u different from zero. Keep original holes after cancellation and restrictions after multiplication by zero.

The logarithm of a sum has no general product-style expansion. Convert different bases before applying same-base identities. One counterexample disproves a universal claim; one matching value does not prove it.
Change of base gives $\log_b A=\ln A/\ln b$. Retain exact expressions until a numerical answer is explicitly requested, then round the final value.

Isolate an exponential before taking logarithms. Its isolated value must be positive. Check for a nonzero x coefficient before dividing; an identity or contradiction can produce all real inputs or none.
For a quadratic substitution $u=b^x$, keep u>0, solve for every candidate u, reject nonpositive candidates, and map every retained value back to x. Repeated roots are listed once.

Solve logarithmic equations on the common original domain. Algebraic candidates are provisional until each original argument and denominator has been checked. A squared argument can produce two valid roots.

The 34 named practice variants cover the planned skills. Each four-item checkpoint samples one critical item from each family. All four selected items must pass independently; one passed form does not establish that every named variant was tested.
retrieval: After a delay, derive the product identity from exponent arithmetic and reconstruct the full-domain expansion of ln((x-2)^2). Give a counterexample to a proposed logarithm sum rule and explain why the canceled point in ln(((x-1)(x-3))/(x-3)) stays excluded. Solve 2^(2x+1)=7 exactly, then solve e^(2x)-5e^x+6=0 while retaining every positive substitution root. Finally solve ln(x-1)+ln(x-3)=ln(8), list every algebraic candidate, and check the original arguments. Repeat with new values and explain the reasons without referring to an answer key.
